newsitem.title: UK: Mark knocked as market reassured on EU pact.
newsitem.headline: Mark knocked as market reassured on EU pact.

text.p: The mark lost ground throughout the European session as players became increasingly optimistic that agreement would be reached on the key EU stability pact.

France set the market buzzing with speculation of a delay to the whole European monetary union project on Monday when it called for time to study the pact -- due to be signed at the Amsterdam summit next week -- before endorsing it.

But a raft of comments from European officials on Wednesday depressed the German unit as the market decided delay was less likely than a broad-based, soft single currency -- a prospect which is traditionally mark-negative.
"There has been some buying of high yielders related to what is perceived to be a greater prospect of a wide euro going ahead on time," said PaineWebber international economist James McKay.
The mark eased to 985.70/6.00 Italian lire and 84.60/61 pesetas by 1428 GMT from late Tuesday's European levels of 988.60/90 and 84.66/69.

European Commission President Jacques Santer said he expected an agreement on the stability pact -- designed to enforce budgetary rigour after EMU begins -- in Amsterdam, while Italian Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini said he thought a deal could be reached in time for the summit or just after it.

Optimism was boosted by French finance minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn, who said France wanted a quick solution to the impasse if possible. On top of that, a government spokeswoman said there was no divergence between Prime Minister Lionel Jospin and President Jacques Chirac on Europe.

Meantime, German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel said France would adhere to the pact and to the strict EMU entry criteria. For its part, Germany was prepared to agree to a jobs chapter in Amsterdam so long as it did not incur extra EU spending, Kinkel said.
He also warned that delaying EMU could kill it.
German Chancellor Helmut Kohl dismissed speculation that changes could be made to the euro timetable. That would spell catastrophe for the German economy, labour market and currency, Kohl warned.

He was responding to a report in the Berliner Morgenpost newspaper that senior officials in his coalition were considering a plan to delay the start of EMU by one year and shorten the transition phase for the euro's introduction.
Overall, traders said the market remained highly jittery as it wavered between the conflicting scenarios of EMU delay and the timely launch of a wide, soft euro.
The coming to power of the left wing in France sparked fears of a broad-based euro as the Socialists have declared their desire to see Spain and Italy in EMU from the start.
Germany's problems in plugging its budget gaps to qualify for EMU have fanned those fears.
